To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

power-sharing institutions are a product of the institutional legacy, that the outcome of the war determines the likelihood of power-sharing arrangements, that power-sharing arrangements are not effective in reducing the risk of civil wars, and that power-sharing with a rebellious region may increase the risk of civil conflict.

power-sharing institutions are largely a consequence of war outcome and institutional legacy, that power-sharing arrangements are largely a consequence institutional legacy, that the risk of a recurrence of civil war is higher when the war outcome is a victory of the government, when the government is not forced to share power, when a grand coalition is not formed, and when the rebels receive autonomy.

(1) power-sharing institutions are more likely to occur when a conflict is governmental rather than territorial; (2) power-sharing arrangements are more likely to emerge when a conflict is territorial rather than governmental; (3) power-sharing institutions have no significant effect on the risk of civil conflict; (4) power-sharing arrangements reduce the risk of civil wars, but only in the case of governmental conflicts; (5) granting autonomy increases the risk of a conflict turning violent again.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question: what is the relationship between power-sharing institutions and the risk of civil conflict?
two main issues: (i) the origins of constitutional choices in the shadow of civil war; (ii) the effectiveness of constitutional choices for the prevention of civil wars.
the question of whether power-sharing is the best choice for a society that has just emerged from civil war.

the choice of a power-sharing institution or arrangement is not an effective way to prevent a war from re-igniting.
